sources.title: 상법 제638조의3 — 보험약관의 교부·설명 의무
sources.excerpt_locator: 제638조의3 제1항·제2항 (조문 전체, 개정연혁 표기 제외)
sources.retrieval_note: Official law.go.kr article page read directly through web retrieval; whitespace normalized.
sources.text: 제638조의3(보험약관의 교부ㆍ설명 의무) ① 보험자는 보험계약을 체결할 때에 보험계약자에게 보험약관을 교부하고 그 약관의 중요한 내용을 설명하여야 한다. ② 보험자가 제1항을 위반한 경우 보험계약자는 보험계약이 성립한 날부터 3개월 이내에 그 계약을 취소할 수 있다.
sources.scope_note: 대한민국 보험계약 체결 시 약관 교부·중요 내용 설명 및 위반 시 취소에 관한 조문이다. 계약 문구만으로 실제 교부·설명 여부나 취소기간의 기산점을 확정하지 않는다. 과거 계약은 적용 시점의 법령을 별도 확인해야 한다.

sources.title: 상법 제651조 — 고지의무위반으로 인한 계약해지
sources.retrieval_note: Official law.go.kr article page read directly through web retrieval; whitespace normalized.
sources.text: 제651조(고지의무위반으로 인한 계약해지) 보험계약당시에 보험계약자 또는 피보험자가 고의 또는 중대한 과실로 인하여 중요한 사항을 고지하지 아니하거나 부실의 고지를 한 때에는 보험자는 그 사실을 안 날로부터 1월내에, 계약을 체결한 날로부터 3년내에 한하여 계약을 해지할 수 있다. 그러나 보험자가 계약당시에 그 사실을 알았거나 중대한 과실로 인하여 알지 못한 때에는 그러하지 아니하다.
sources.scope_note: 계약 체결 당시 중요한 사항의 불고지·부실고지, 고의·중과실, 보험자의 인식 및 해지기간이 문제되는 경우에 한정한다. 단순한 불리한 약관이나 모든 고지 누락을 곧바로 적법한 해지 사유로 판정하지 않는다.

sources.title: 상법 제652조 — 위험변경증가의 통지와 계약해지
sources.excerpt_locator: 제652조 제1항·제2항 (조문 전체, 개정연혁 표기 제외)
sources.retrieval_note: Official law.go.kr article page read directly through web retrieval; whitespace normalized.
sources.text: 제652조(위험변경증가의 통지와 계약해지) ①보험기간 중에 보험계약자 또는 피보험자가 사고발생의 위험이 현저하게 변경 또는 증가된 사실을 안 때에는 지체없이 보험자에게 통지하여야 한다. 이를 해태한 때에는 보험자는 그 사실을 안 날로부터 1월내에 한하여 계약을 해지할 수 있다. ②보험자가 제1항의 위험변경증가의 통지를 받은 때에는 1월내에 보험료의 증액을 청구하거나 계약을 해지할 수 있다.
sources.scope_note: 보험기간 중 위험의 현저한 변경·증가와 그 인식·통지가 전제된다. 계약 체결 전 고지의무와 구별하며, 모든 직업·생활 변화가 이 조문의 요건을 충족한다고 추정하지 않는다.

sources.title: 상법 제655조 — 계약해지와 보험금청구권
sources.retrieval_note: Official law.go.kr article page verified by direct HTTPS HTML retrieval; whitespace normalized.
sources.text: 제655조(계약해지와 보험금청구권) 보험사고가 발생한 후라도 보험자가 제650조, 제651조, 제652조 및 제653조에 따라 계약을 해지하였을 때에는 보험금을 지급할 책임이 없고 이미 지급한 보험금의 반환을 청구할 수 있다. 다만, 고지의무(告知義務)를 위반한 사실 또는 위험이 현저하게 변경되거나 증가된 사실이 보험사고 발생에 영향을 미치지 아니하였음이 증명된 경우에는 보험금을 지급할 책임이 있다.
sources.scope_note: 열거된 조문에 따른 해지와 보험사고 이후 지급책임을 다룬다. 단서의 인과관계 예외를 생략해서는 안 된다. 약관만으로 고지 위반, 적법한 해지 또는 보험사고와의 인과관계를 확정하지 않는다.

sources.title: 상법 제662조 — 소멸시효
sources.retrieval_note: Official law.go.kr article page verified by direct HTTPS HTML retrieval; whitespace normalized.
sources.text: 제662조(소멸시효) 보험금청구권은 3년간, 보험료 또는 적립금의 반환청구권은 3년간, 보험료청구권은 2년간 행사하지 아니하면 시효의 완성으로 소멸한다.
sources.scope_note: 권리 유형별 소멸시효 기간에 관한 조문이다. 실제 기산점, 시효 중단·정지 및 경과규정은 이 짧은 조문만으로 결정할 수 없다. 계약상 청구 절차나 제출기한을 법정 소멸시효와 자동으로 동일시하지 않는다.

sources.title: 상법 제663조 — 보험계약자 등의 불이익변경금지
sources.retrieval_note: Official law.go.kr article page verified by direct HTTPS HTML retrieval after web fetch errors; whitespace normalized.
sources.text: 제663조(보험계약자 등의 불이익변경금지) 이 편의 규정은 당사자간의 특약으로 보험계약자 또는 피보험자나 보험수익자의 불이익으로 변경하지 못한다. 그러나 재보험 및 해상보험 기타 이와 유사한 보험의 경우에는 그러하지 아니하다.
sources.scope_note: 상법 보험편 규정의 불이익 변경 금지이며 재보험·해상보험 등 명시적 예외가 있다. 모든 불리한 보험 약관이 이 조문에 위반되는 것은 아니다. 변경 대상 법정 규정, 보호대상자와 보험 종류를 특정해야 한다.

sources.title: 12 CFR §1026.5 — General disclosure requirements
sources.source_version: CFPB page labeled current regulation on access; not a historical-contract applicability determination.
sources.retrieval_note: Official CFPB regulation text; interpretive commentary excluded; selected paragraph labels expanded for unambiguous location.
sources.text:
(a)(1)(i) The creditor shall make the disclosures required by this subpart clearly and conspicuously.
(a)(2)(i) Terminology used in providing the disclosures required by this subpart shall be consistent.
(b)(1)(i) General rule. The creditor shall furnish account-opening disclosures required by §1026.6 before the first transaction is made under the plan.
sources.scope_note: Selected disclosure form and timing rules for covered open-end consumer credit. This is not the complete section; exceptions and special timing rules appear elsewhere. Absence from an extracted agreement does not establish that a separate required disclosure was never delivered. Not a general rule for commercial-purpose loans.

sources.title: 12 CFR §1026.6(b)(2)(i) — Account-opening APR disclosures
sources.source_version: CFPB page labeled current regulation on access; not a historical-contract applicability determination.
sources.retrieval_note: Official CFPB regulation text, excluding embedded interpretive commentary; whitespace normalized.
sources.text:
(i) Annual percentage rate. Each periodic rate that may be used to compute the finance charge on an outstanding balance for purchases, a cash advance, or a balance transfer, expressed as an annual percentage rate (as determined by §1026.14(b)). When more than one rate applies for a category of transactions, the range of balances to which each rate is applicable shall also be disclosed. The annual percentage rate for purchases disclosed pursuant to this paragraph shall be in at least 16-point type, except for the following: A penalty rate that may apply upon the occurrence of one or more specific events.
(A) Variable-rate information. If a rate disclosed under paragraph (b)(2)(i) of this section is a variable rate, the creditor shall also disclose the fact that the rate may vary and how the rate is determined. In describing how the applicable rate will be determined, the creditor must identify the type of index or formula that is used in setting the rate.
sources.scope_note: Applies within account-opening disclosures for covered open-end, not home-secured plans. This excerpt stops before additional table-content restrictions in (A) and omits other subsections. It does not set a maximum interest rate or establish that an APR increase is lawful. Plain-text extraction cannot establish font-size compliance.

sources.title: 12 CFR §1026.9(c)(2)(i)(A) — Advance notice of significant changes
sources.source_version: CFPB page labeled current regulation on access; not a historical-contract applicability determination.
sources.retrieval_note: Official CFPB regulation text; this excerpt intentionally retains references to exceptions.
sources.text: (A) General. For plans other than home-equity plans subject to the requirements of §1026.40, except as provided in paragraphs (c)(2)(i)(B), (c)(2)(iii) and (c)(2)(v) of this section, when a significant change in account terms as described in paragraph (c)(2)(ii) of this section is made, a creditor must provide a written notice of the change at least 45 days prior to the effective date of the change to each consumer who may be affected. The 45-day timing requirement does not apply if the consumer has agreed to a particular change as described in paragraph (c)(2)(i)(B) of this section; for such changes, notice must be given in accordance with the timing requirements of paragraph (c)(2)(i)(B) of this section.
sources.scope_note: For covered open-end, not home-secured plans and changes meeting the section's definition. The text expressly cross-references exceptions. Do not claim every rate or fee change requires 45 days, or infer actual notice delivery from the agreement alone. Other penalty-rate events are addressed in paragraph (g), not reproduced here.

sources.title: 12 CFR §1026.13(c) — Billing-error resolution timing
sources.source_version: CFPB page labeled current regulation on access; not a historical-contract applicability determination.
sources.retrieval_note: Official CFPB regulation text; embedded interpretive commentary excluded.
sources.text:
(c) Time for resolution; general procedures.
(1) The creditor shall mail or deliver written acknowledgment to the consumer within 30 days of receiving a billing error notice, unless the creditor has complied with the appropriate resolution procedures of paragraphs (e) and (f) of this section, as applicable, within the 30-day period; and
(2) The creditor shall comply with the appropriate resolution procedures of paragraphs (e) and (f) of this section, as applicable, within 2 complete billing cycles (but in no event later than 90 days) after receiving a billing error notice.
sources.scope_note: Presupposes a billing error and qualifying consumer notice under (a) and (b); it does not cover every customer complaint. The notice requirements, including the applicable 60-day period, and substantive resolution procedures are not fully reproduced. Do not infer that a contractual dispute is necessarily a covered billing error.

sources.title: 12 CFR §1026.52(a) — First-year fee limitation and exceptions
sources.source_version: CFPB page labeled current regulation on access; this entry does not reproduce penalty-fee safe-harbor dollar amounts.
sources.retrieval_note: Official CFPB regulation text; embedded interpretive commentary excluded.
sources.text:
(1) General rule. Except as provided in paragraph (a)(2) of this section, the total amount of fees a consumer is required to pay with respect to a credit card account under an open-end (not home-secured) consumer credit plan during the first year after account opening must not exceed 25 percent of the credit limit in effect when the account is opened. For purposes of this paragraph, an account is considered open no earlier than the date on which the account may first be used by the consumer to engage in transactions.
(2) Fees not subject to limitations. Paragraph (a) of this section does not apply to: (i) Late payment fees, over-the-limit fees, and returned-payment fees; or (ii) Fees that the consumer is not required to pay with respect to the account.
(3) Rule of construction. Paragraph (a) of this section does not authorize the imposition or payment of fees or charges otherwise prohibited by law.
sources.scope_note: Only the first-year limitation and its expressly listed exceptions are included. This is not a cap of 25 percent on every fee and not a penalty-fee safe-harbor rule. Determine account-opening date, initial credit limit, fee classification, and covered consumer-account status before considering application.

sources.title: 12 CFR §1026.55(a)-(b) — APR, fee, and charge increases
sources.excerpt_locator: 1026.55(a) and introductory paragraph of (b); exception conditions not reproduced
sources.source_version: CFPB page labeled current regulation on access; not a historical-contract applicability determination.
sources.retrieval_note: Official CFPB regulation text; embedded interpretive commentary excluded.
sources.text:
(a) General rule. Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, a card issuer must not increase an annual percentage rate or a fee or charge required to be disclosed under §1026.6(b)(2)(ii), (b)(2)(iii), or (b)(2)(xii) on a credit card account under an open-end (not home-secured) consumer credit plan.
(b) Exceptions. A card issuer may increase an annual percentage rate or a fee or charge required to be disclosed under §1026.6(b)(2)(ii), (b)(2)(iii), or (b)(2)(xii) pursuant to an exception set forth in this paragraph even if that increase would not be permitted under a different exception.
sources.scope_note: Covered consumer credit card accounts only. The detailed exceptions in (b), including variable-rate, notice, delinquency, and other conditions, are not reproduced; a permissible exception must not be presumed absent. This general prohibition alone cannot establish that a particular contractual increase violates the regulation.

sources.title: 11 U.S.C. §506(b) — Interest, fees, costs, and charges on oversecured claims
sources.source_version: OLRC preliminary edition primary-source index states laws in effect on July 17, 2026.
sources.retrieval_note: Statutory wording verified in the search index of the official uscode.house.gov page. Direct page requests timed out; no claim of a successful fresh full-page download or September 5 legal currency.
sources.text: (b) To the extent that an allowed secured claim is secured by property the value of which, after any recovery under subsection (c) of this section, is greater than the amount of such claim, there shall be allowed to the holder of such claim, interest on such claim, and any reasonable fees, costs, or charges provided for under the agreement or State statute under which such claim arose.
sources.scope_note: Concerns allowance on an oversecured claim in bankruptcy; collateral value, allowed-claim status, agreement or state-statute terms, and reasonableness matter. Not a general ban on commercial loan fees and not a universal outside-bankruptcy rule. Do not presume a loan is oversecured or that bankruptcy is pending.

sources.title: 11 U.S.C. §552(a), (b)(1) — Postpetition effect of security interest
sources.source_version: OLRC preliminary edition primary-source index states laws in effect on August 4, 2026.
sources.retrieval_note: Statutory wording verified in the search index of the official uscode.house.gov page. Direct page requests timed out; no claim of a successful fresh full-page download or September 5 legal currency.
sources.text:
(a) Except as provided in subsection (b) of this section, property acquired by the estate or by the debtor after the commencement of the case is not subject to any lien resulting from any security agreement entered into by the debtor before the commencement of the case.
(b)(1) Except as provided in sections 363, 506(c), 522, 544, 545, 547, and 548 of this title, if the debtor and an entity entered into a security agreement before the commencement of the case and if the security interest created by such security agreement extends to property of the debtor acquired before the commencement of the case and to proceeds, products, offspring, or profits of such property, then such security interest extends to such proceeds, products, offspring, or profits acquired by the estate after the commencement of the case to the extent provided by such security agreement and by applicable nonbankruptcy law, except to any extent that the court, after notice and a hearing and based on the equities of the case, orders otherwise.
sources.scope_note: A bankruptcy-specific rule governing postpetition property and prepetition security agreements. The quoted proceeds exception and cross-references are substantive; subsection (b)(2) adds another exception not reproduced here. This does not invalidate all after-acquired-property clauses outside bankruptcy.

sources.title: 6 Del. C. §9-602 — Waiver and variance of rights and duties
sources.excerpt_locator: 9-602 introductory language and items (6), (7), (11); remaining listed items omitted
sources.source_version: Delaware Code Online Article 9, Part 6 page retrieved on the access date; no independent effective-date certification.
sources.retrieval_note: Official Delaware Code enactment text, not the model UCC; selected noncontiguous provisions with whitespace normalized.
sources.scope_note: Delaware enactment only, and only when the relevant Delaware Article 9 provisions govern the transaction and issue. Not federal law or automatically the law of another U.S. state. The exception in 9-624 and omitted listed provisions require full-source review. A Delaware incorporation address alone does not decide every choice-of-law issue. If jurisdiction does not match, relevance is zero.

sources.title: 6 Del. C. §9-607(c)-(e) — Collection and enforcement by secured party
sources.source_version: Delaware Code Online Article 9, Part 6 page retrieved on the access date; no independent effective-date certification.
sources.retrieval_note: Official Delaware Code enactment text, not the model UCC; whitespace normalized.
sources.text:
(c) Commercially reasonable collection and enforcement. — A secured party shall proceed in a commercially reasonable manner if the secured party: (1) undertakes to collect from or enforce an obligation of an account debtor or other person obligated on collateral; and (2) is entitled to charge back uncollected collateral or otherwise to full or limited recourse against the debtor or a secondary obligor.
(d) Expenses of collection and enforcement. — A secured party may deduct from the collections made pursuant to subsection (c) reasonable expenses of collection and enforcement, including reasonable attorney’s fees and legal expenses incurred by the secured party.
(e) Duties to secured party not affected. — This section does not determine whether an account debtor, bank, or other person obligated on collateral owes a duty to a secured party.
sources.scope_note: Delaware Article 9 collection/enforcement of obligations on collateral, with the conditions in (c); not a universal rule for all creditor collection or unsecured-loan fees. Applicable governing law and secured-transaction facts must be established independently. If Delaware jurisdiction does not match, relevance is zero.

sources.title: 6 Del. C. §9-610(a)-(c) — Disposition of collateral after default
sources.source_version: Delaware Code Online Article 9, Part 6 page retrieved on the access date; no independent effective-date certification.
sources.retrieval_note: Official Delaware Code enactment text, not the model UCC; whitespace normalized.
sources.text:
(a) Disposition after default. — After default, a secured party may sell, lease, license, or otherwise dispose of any or all of the collateral in its present condition or following any commercially reasonable preparation or processing.
(b) Commercially reasonable disposition. — Every aspect of a disposition of collateral, including the method, manner, time, place, and other terms, must be commercially reasonable. If commercially reasonable, a secured party may dispose of collateral by public or private proceedings, by one or more contracts, as a unit or in parcels, and at any time and place and on any terms.
(c) Purchase by secured party. — A secured party may purchase collateral: (1) at a public disposition; or (2) at a private disposition only if the collateral is of a kind that is customarily sold on a recognized market or the subject of widely distributed standard price quotations.
sources.scope_note: Delaware Article 9 collateral disposition after default, subject to other Article 9 requirements. A private sale is not categorically unlawful and contractual discretion does not establish how an actual sale occurred. Not automatically applicable to other states, unsecured loans, or every real-property foreclosure. If Delaware jurisdiction does not match, relevance is zero.

sources.title: N.Y. General Obligations Law §5-1401 — Choice of law
sources.source_version: Official New York Senate page labels its most recent revision as August 31, 2018; retrieved on the access date.
sources.retrieval_note: Official New York legislation page read directly. Whitespace normalized; the official text's double hyphen in 1--301 is preserved.
sources.text:
§ 5-1401. Choice of law. 1. The parties to any contract, agreement or undertaking, contingent or otherwise, in consideration of, or relating to any obligation arising out of a transaction covering in the aggregate not less than two hundred fifty thousand dollars, including a transaction otherwise covered by subsection (a) of section 1--301 of the uniform commercial code, may agree that the law of this state shall govern their rights and duties in whole or in part, whether or not such contract, agreement or undertaking bears a reasonable relation to this state. This section shall not apply to any contract, agreement or undertaking (a) for labor or personal services, (b) relating to any transaction for personal, family or household services, or (c) to the extent provided to the contrary in subsection (c) of section 1--301 of the uniform commercial code.
2. Nothing contained in this section shall be construed to limit or deny the enforcement of any provision respecting choice of law in any other contract, agreement or undertaking.
sources.scope_note: New York choice-of-law statute with an aggregate transaction threshold of at least $250,000, an agreement selecting New York law, and express labor/personal-services, personal/family/household-services, and UCC exceptions. It does not establish a consumer-protection prohibition. Subsection (2) means a below-threshold choice-of-law provision is not automatically unenforceable. A New York connection alone does not prove these conditions; a jurisdiction mismatch receives relevance zero and unresolved applicability is recorded as uncertain.

sources.title: N.Y. General Obligations Law §5-1402 — Choice of forum
sources.source_version: Official New York Senate page labels its most recent revision as September 22, 2014; retrieved on the access date.
sources.retrieval_note: Official New York legislation page read directly; whitespace normalized.
sources.text:
§ 5-1402. Choice of forum. 1. Notwithstanding any act which limits or affects the right of a person to maintain an action or proceeding, including, but not limited to, paragraph (b) of section thirteen hundred fourteen of the business corporation law and subdivision two of section two hundred-b of the banking law, any person may maintain an action or proceeding against a foreign corporation, non-resident, or foreign state where the action or proceeding arises out of or relates to any contract, agreement or undertaking for which a choice of New York law has been made in whole or in part pursuant to section 5-1401 and which (a) is a contract, agreement or undertaking, contingent or otherwise, in consideration of, or relating to any obligation arising out of a transaction covering in the aggregate, not less than one million dollars, and (b) which contains a provision or provisions whereby such foreign corporation or non-resident agrees to submit to the jurisdiction of the courts of this state.
2. Nothing contained in this section shall be construed to affect the enforcement of any provision respecting choice of forum in any other contract, agreement or undertaking.
sources.scope_note: New York forum statute for the specified actions: requires a choice of New York law pursuant to 5-1401, aggregate transaction of at least $1 million, and the specified submission to New York courts. It is not a general ban on foreign forums or a universal consumer-loan right. Subsection (2) preserves other forum provisions rather than automatically invalidating below-threshold agreements. Independently check each statutory condition; a jurisdiction mismatch receives relevance zero and unresolved applicability is recorded as uncertain.
